summary: Defines how to carry IPv6 packets over PPP links, including the IPv6 Control Protocol used to set up and configure IPv6 on a link. It describes how the two ends negotiate interface identifiers. It is a draft standard, a standards-track status.

eli5.summary: PPP is like a single wire between two computers. This explains how those two computers agree to speak IPv6 over that wire and set up their addresses.

questions: how does ipv6 work over ppp
how is the ppp interface identifier negotiated
what is the ppp protocol number for ipv6
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree to carry IPv6, pick interface identifiers and form link-local addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to run over point-to-point PPP links, including how the two ends set it up and obtain unique address parts.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets ride in PPP frames with Protocol type 0057, and a Network Control Protocol, IPV6CP, negotiates a 64-bit interface identifier that forms the link-local address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5072 obsoletes RFC 2472 and is updated by RFC 8064. It also says duplicate address detection can be redundant under two stated conditions.

today: RFC 5072 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2472 and is updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: PPP and IPv6 Together
sections.content:
PPP has three components: a method of encapsulating datagrams over serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring network-layer protocols. Each end first sends LCP packets, then NCP packets, and only then can datagrams flow.

This RFC defines the NCP for IPv6, called the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP). It also defines how IPv6 packets are sent over PPP and how link-local addresses are formed. It obsoletes RFC 2472.
sections.eli5: First the two ends say hello and agree on the basics. Then they agree on which languages to speak, and IPv6 is one of them.

sections.title: Sending IPv6 Datagrams
sections.content:
Before any IPv6 packet is sent, PPP MUST reach the network-layer protocol phase and IPV6CP MUST reach the Opened state. Exactly one IPv6 packet goes into the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 0057.

The maximum IPv6 packet length equals the maximum length of the PPP Information field. PPP links supporting IPv6 MUST allow the Information field to be at least as large as the minimum link MTU required for IPv6 in RFC 2460.
sections.eli5: Each PPP envelope holds exactly one IPv6 letter, and the envelope is stamped with a special code so everyone knows it is IPv6.

sections.title: The IPv6 Control Protocol
sections.content:
IPV6CP configures, enables and disables the IPv6 modules at both ends. It is exactly the same as LCP (RFC 1661) with a few exceptions. Its packets use Protocol type hex 8057. Only Codes 1 through 7 are used (Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject); other Codes should get a Code-Reject.

IPV6CP packets received before the network-layer protocol phase should be silently discarded. Implementations should be prepared to wait for authentication and link quality determination to finish before timing out, and give up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time. IPV6CP also has its own set of configuration options.
sections.eli5: The setup conversation follows the same script as the first hello, with a few lines changed and its own envelope stamp.

sections.title: The Interface Identifier Option
sections.content:
The only option defined here is Type 1, Interface-Identifier. It negotiates a unique 64-bit interface identifier for address autoconfiguration at the local end. A Configure-Request MUST contain exactly one instance, and the two ends MUST end up with different values.

A node picks a tentative identifier in this preference order: (1) derive it from an IEEE EUI-48 or EUI-64 identifier, changing only the universal/local "u" bit (an EUI-48 first gets 0xFF and 0xFE inserted in the middle); (2) use another source of uniqueness, such as link-layer addresses or serial numbers, with the u bit set to zero; (3) generate a random number, again with the u bit zero. If no good source exists, a zero value may be sent and the peer may suggest one.

The receiver compares the value with its own last Configure-Request. A different non-zero value is acknowledged. A zero value, or one equal to its own, gets a Configure-Nak suggesting a different non-zero value. If both are zero, a Configure-Reject with zero ends the negotiation, since no unique identifier can be negotiated. By default an implementation SHOULD try to negotiate its identifier. If none is negotiated, recovery is unspecified; manual configuration is one approach.
sections.eli5: Each end must pick a name tag, and the two tags must differ. If both pick the same one, one end suggests a new tag until they are different.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Duplicate Detection
sections.content:
The negotiated identifier is used to autoconfigure the IPv6 link-local address of the PPP interface. That address is the 10-bit prefix 1111111010 (FE80::), then 54 zero bits, then the 64-bit Interface-Identifier. The same identifier SHOULD NOT be assumed for global unicast addresses; a peer MAY generate one or more other identifiers, for instance by the privacy method in RFC 4941.

Because the identifier is negotiated in IPV6CP, running duplicate address detection (DAD) on the link-local address is redundant. DAD on global addresses may also be redundant if two conditions hold: the prefixes the access router advertises are exclusive to the PPP link, and the router does not autoconfigure global addresses from those prefixes. In that case it is RECOMMENDED that the DupAddrDetectTransmits default be zero. The RFC gives 3GPP2 and 3GPP networks as examples.
sections.eli5: Since the name tags were already checked to be different, nobody needs to shout "is anyone else using this name?" again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Lack of link security, such as authentication, raises the concerns of stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862) for global addresses built from negotiated or generated identifiers. The RFC lists three appropriate PPP mechanisms: access control lists to filter traffic, an authentication protocol negotiated between peers, and an encryption protocol for confidentiality.

Threats remain even with these in place. For example, MD5 authentication exposes one to replay of a station's identity and password hash. Readers are pointed to RFC 3748 for a generic threat model.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can plug into the string can pretend to be someone. Passwords, filters and secret codes help, but none is perfect.

sections.title: IANA and Changes from RFC 2472
sections.content: IANA assigned value 1 for the Type field of the interface-identifier option. Compared with RFC 2472, this RFC removed the IPv6-Compression-Protocol section on IESG recommendation and moved it to a separate standards-track document. It also lets global addresses use identifiers generated by a peer, not only negotiated ones, and identifies cases where DAD can be skipped. Appendix A explains that global addresses come from stateless autoconfiguration using router-advertised prefixes, or from stateful autoconfiguration such as DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: This is the updated edition. One chapter was moved to its own book, and some rules about name tags were made more flexible.

fields.name: Interface-Identifier
fields.desc: 64-bit identifier, or zero if no good source of uniqueness exists.
